hypothesis: The neuron responds strongly to high-contrast, dark structural forms—typically elongated vertical lines, stripes, or distinct silhouettes—centered against a uniform, light-colored background. The activating features are consistently black, deep charcoal, or dark gray (e.g., the segmented body of a centipede, a lamp pole, clock hands, or a deep shadow crease), set against a contrasting background of light gray, off-white, or silver. The unit demonstrates a specific preference for monochromatic or grayscale imagery, remaining invariant to object identity (activating for biological specimens, mechanical parts, and geometric shadows alike) as long as the sharp dark-on-light contrast is preserved. The activating element typically spans 30–70% of the image height and is most often aligned along or near the central vertical axis.

natural.description: Centered against a grainy, monochromatic light gray background stands a house centipede, viewed from a top-down perspective. Radiating from the sides of this body are numerous pairs of long, spindly legs—approximately 15 on each side—that arch outwards and downwards. These appendages exhibit a subtle banding pattern of alternating dark and light gray segments. The legs at the anterior (top) end are shorter, extending roughly 15% of the image width away from the body, while the legs progressively lengthen towards the posterior (bottom). The final pair of rear legs is exceptionally long and thread-like, trailing downwards and diverging slightly to mimic the appearance of antennae, fading into the background near the bottom edge. At the head, two long, thin antennae project upwards in a V-shape; the left antenna extends almost vertically, while the right antenna angles approximately 45 degrees towards the upper right. Faint, soft shadows fall to the left of the legs and body, suggesting a diffuse light source positioned to the right, and the entire scene has a soft focus, blurring the fine tips of the appendages into the surrounding gray space.
